case_info.scenario: A woman in her 70s with rheumatoid arthritis who was receiving long-term immunosuppression (prednisolone and methotrexate) presented with a 6-month history of progressive papulonodules on her face and extremities. The patient, an avid gardener with regular soil exposure, reported no systemic symptoms, such as fever, cough, or weight loss. Initial laboratory investigations, including a complete blood cell count and biochemical tests, yielded unremarkable results. HIV screening results were negative, and chest computed tomography showed no evidence of pulmonary involvement. Physical examination revealed multiple papules and nodules, with seropurulent crusts on the face, dorsal hands, and extremities alongside rheumatoid joint deformities (Figure 1A). No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Histopathological examination of lesional biopsy specimens from the face and hand showed identical features (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Firm papules and nodules with seropurulent crusts on the dorsal hands, along with joint deformities. B, Diffuse dermal spindle cells with focal vaguely storiform architecture, along with sparse lymphocytic and neutrophilic infiltrates (hematoxylin-eosin staining; original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: C. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor Histopathological examination of the right hand revealed diffuse dermal spindle cell proliferation with focal storiform architecture, accompanied by sparse mixed inflammatory infiltrates composed of lymphocytes and neutrophils (Figure 1B). Scattered foam cells and epithelioid histiocytes were present without evidence of significant mitotic activity, necrosis, or cellular atypia. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the spindle cells were positive for CD68 but negative for factor XIIIa, desmin, smooth muscle actin (SMA), CD34, S-100, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK). Special stains were negative for fungal organisms (periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott methenamine silver), and there were numerous acid-fast bacilli within spindle cells (Figure 2).Mycobacterium hemophilumwas isolated at 4 weeks and confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Based on findings, the diagnosis of cutaneous mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor was made. The patient received triple therapy with clarithromycin, rifampin, and moxifloxacin. At 6-month follow-up, there was near-complete lesion resolution. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor (MSP) is a rare condition characterized by the proliferation of spindle-shaped histiocytes containing abundant acid-fast bacilli, primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals.1While lymph nodes are the most common site, extranodal involvement has been documented in skin, soft tissue, and visceral organs.2To date, approximately 10 cases of cutaneous MSP have been reported, with most associated withMycobacterium aviumcomplex.3We present the first case of cutaneous MSP caused byM hemophilum.M hemophilumis a fastidious, slow-growing nontuberculous mycobacterium (NTM) that inhabits water sources and soil. While this patient denied direct water exposure, she reported gardening activities with substantial contact with soil and potted plants. The clinical presentation, characterized by localized cutaneous lesions in trauma-prone areas, absence of systemic symptoms, unremarkable laboratory findings, and negative imaging results, suggested direct cutaneous inoculation during gardening vs hematogenous dissemination.M hemophiluminfection typically manifests in immunocompromised hosts, with cutaneous findings, including nodules, pustules, and ulcerations, affecting the extremities.4Histopathologically, similar to other NTMs,M hemophiluminfection generally exhibits a suppurative, granulomatous inflammatory pattern with variable caseation necrosis.5Therefore, the unusual presentation of the spindle cell pseudotumor in this case created diagnostic challenges. The initial clinical differential diagnosis included rheumatoid arthritis–related skin manifestations (eg, rheumatoid nodules, rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis) and infectious causes. Histopathological examination excluded rheumatoid nodules due to the absence of palisading granulomas with central fibrinoid necrosis and ruled out rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis because of the lack of dense neutrophilic infiltrates. The spindle cell–dominated appearance led to consideration of various mesenchymal tumors, such as dermatofibroma, nodular fasciitis, and inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor. Dermatofibroma was excluded because the spindle cells tested negative for factor XIIIa. Nodular fasciitis typically shows a tissue culture–like growth pattern, loosely arranged feathery fascicles of plump fibroblasts/myofibroblasts, extravasated erythrocytes, and SMA immunoreactivity,6which were not observed in this case. The negative results for desmin, SMA, and ALK did not support a diagnosis of inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor.7While Kaposi sarcoma remained a consideration, the absence of pathognomonic features, including vascular slit formation, mitotic activity, and hyaline globules, excluded this diagnosis. Clues that favor a diagnosis of this inflammatory infectious lesion vs neoplasia include the presence of admixed neutrophilic inflammation, neutrophilic microabscesses, foamy macrophages, and peripheral granulomatous inflammation. For a patient with impaired immunity and a spindle cell lesion, these findings may lead to special stains or PCR.2 The pathogenesis of MSP remains incompletely understood but likely involves altered host-pathogen interactions in immunocompromised states. The spindled cells exhibit monocyte/macrophage origin, reflecting dysregulated macrophage polarization: proinflammatory M1 macrophages contribute to spindle cell proliferation and granuloma formation, while anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages promote fibrosis. Chronic NTM infection with impaired T-cell responses is associated with immature granuloma development. MSP demonstrates mixed M1/M2 features, highlighting macrophage plasticity.2Long-term corticosteroid and methotrexate therapy likely contributed to histiocytic proliferation and failed mycobacterial containment. Treating MSP involves surgical intervention and antimycobacterial therapy tailored to the extent and host immunity. For immunocompetent patients with localized cutaneous lesions, complete surgical excision may be curative. However, immunocompromised individuals or those with disseminated disease require prolonged combination antibiotic therapy (6-12 months for cutaneous disease and 12-18 months for systemic involvement). Given this patient’s disseminated cutaneous disease, we initiated standard oral triple therapy, combining fluoroquinolone, macrolide, and rifampin, the first-line regimen forM hemophiluminfection.8

[Role]
You are a senior clinician (the Doctor) trying to make a clinical decision about the given patient case.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.


[Information Sparsity]
You share case details, findings, and your reasoning FREELY and PROACTIVELY: when
responding, volunteer relevant information beyond just what was directly asked, to help
move the discussion along.


[Current Context]
- You have examined the patient case.
- Form your own clinical judgment.

[Task]
Based on the case below, state your initial decision and reasoning.

[Expression Style]
- Keep your response under 5 sentences.
- Focus on clinical evidence.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your opening message stating your initial decision and reasoning -- this is
    the only field the AI partner sees",
  "belief": "the clinical decision you have independently made",
  "confidence": "a number between 0 and 1 for how confident you are in that belief (0 = no
    confidence at all, 1 = completely certain) -- your own internal state, not shown to the AI",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why (your terse internal justification,
    separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

Case:
A woman in her 70s with rheumatoid arthritis who was receiving long-term immunosuppression (prednisolone and methotrexate) presented with a 6-month history of progressive papulonodules on her face and extremities. The patient, an avid gardener with regular soil exposure, reported no systemic symptoms, such as fever, cough, or weight loss. Initial laboratory investigations, including a complete blood cell count and biochemical tests, yielded unremarkable results. HIV screening results were negative, and chest computed tomography showed no evidence of pulmonary involvement. Physical examination revealed multiple papules and nodules, with seropurulent crusts on the face, dorsal hands, and extremities alongside rheumatoid joint deformities (Figure 1A). No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Histopathological examination of lesional biopsy specimens from the face and hand showed identical features (Figure 1B).

Image Explanation:
A, Firm papules and nodules with seropurulent crusts on the dorsal hands, along with joint deformities. B, Diffuse dermal spindle cells with focal vaguely storiform architecture, along with sparse lymphocytic and neutrophilic infiltrates (hematoxylin-eosin staining; original magnification ×100).

[Question]
What is the most appropriate next step in management?

Options:
  A. Rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis
  B. Inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor
  C. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor
  D. Kaposi sarcoma

[Instruction]
State your independent clinical decision and reasoning. Start the conversation.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.

case_info.explanation: C. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor Histopathological examination of the right hand revealed diffuse dermal spindle cell proliferation with focal storiform architecture, accompanied by sparse mixed inflammatory infiltrates composed of lymphocytes and neutrophils (Figure 1B). Scattered foam cells and epithelioid histiocytes were present without evidence of significant mitotic activity, necrosis, or cellular atypia. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the spindle cells were positive for CD68 but negative for factor XIIIa, desmin, smooth muscle actin (SMA), CD34, S-100, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK). Special stains were negative for fungal organisms (periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott methenamine silver), and there were numerous acid-fast bacilli within spindle cells (Figure 2).Mycobacterium hemophilumwas isolated at 4 weeks and confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Based on findings, the diagnosis of cutaneous mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor was made. The patient received triple therapy with clarithromycin, rifampin, and moxifloxacin. At 6-month follow-up, there was near-complete lesion resolution. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor (MSP) is a rare condition characterized by the proliferation of spindle-shaped histiocytes containing abundant acid-fast bacilli, primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals.1While lymph nodes are the most common site, extranodal involvement has been documented in skin, soft tissue, and visceral organs.2To date, approximately 10 cases of cutaneous MSP have been reported, with most associated withMycobacterium aviumcomplex.3We present the first case of cutaneous MSP caused byM hemophilum.M hemophilumis a fastidious, slow-growing nontuberculous mycobacterium (NTM) that inhabits water sources and soil. While this patient denied direct water exposure, she reported gardening activities with substantial contact with soil and potted plants. The clinical presentation, characterized by localized cutaneous lesions in trauma-prone areas, absence of systemic symptoms, unremarkable laboratory findings, and negative imaging results, suggested direct cutaneous inoculation during gardening vs hematogenous dissemination.M hemophiluminfection typically manifests in immunocompromised hosts, with cutaneous findings, including nodules, pustules, and ulcerations, affecting the extremities.4Histopathologically, similar to other NTMs,M hemophiluminfection generally exhibits a suppurative, granulomatous inflammatory pattern with variable caseation necrosis.5Therefore, the unusual presentation of the spindle cell pseudotumor in this case created diagnostic challenges. The initial clinical differential diagnosis included rheumatoid arthritis–related skin manifestations (eg, rheumatoid nodules, rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis) and infectious causes. Histopathological examination excluded rheumatoid nodules due to the absence of palisading granulomas with central fibrinoid necrosis and ruled out rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis because of the lack of dense neutrophilic infiltrates. The spindle cell–dominated appearance led to consideration of various mesenchymal tumors, such as dermatofibroma, nodular fasciitis, and inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor. Dermatofibroma was excluded because the spindle cells tested negative for factor XIIIa. Nodular fasciitis typically shows a tissue culture–like growth pattern, loosely arranged feathery fascicles of plump fibroblasts/myofibroblasts, extravasated erythrocytes, and SMA immunoreactivity,6which were not observed in this case. The negative results for desmin, SMA, and ALK did not support a diagnosis of inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor.7While Kaposi sarcoma remained a consideration, the absence of pathognomonic features, including vascular slit formation, mitotic activity, and hyaline globules, excluded this diagnosis. Clues that favor a diagnosis of this inflammatory infectious lesion vs neoplasia include the presence of admixed neutrophilic inflammation, neutrophilic microabscesses, foamy macrophages, and peripheral granulomatous inflammation. For a patient with impaired immunity and a spindle cell lesion, these findings may lead to special stains or PCR.2 The pathogenesis of MSP remains incompletely understood but likely involves altered host-pathogen interactions in immunocompromised states. The spindled cells exhibit monocyte/macrophage origin, reflecting dysregulated macrophage polarization: proinflammatory M1 macrophages contribute to spindle cell proliferation and granuloma formation, while anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages promote fibrosis. Chronic NTM infection with impaired T-cell responses is associated with immature granuloma development. MSP demonstrates mixed M1/M2 features, highlighting macrophage plasticity.2Long-term corticosteroid and methotrexate therapy likely contributed to histiocytic proliferation and failed mycobacterial containment. Treating MSP involves surgical intervention and antimycobacterial therapy tailored to the extent and host immunity. For immunocompetent patients with localized cutaneous lesions, complete surgical excision may be curative. However, immunocompromised individuals or those with disseminated disease require prolonged combination antibiotic therapy (6-12 months for cutaneous disease and 12-18 months for systemic involvement). Given this patient’s disseminated cutaneous disease, we initiated standard oral triple therapy, combining fluoroquinolone, macrolide, and rifampin, the first-line regimen forM hemophiluminfection.8

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: C. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor Histopathological examination of the right hand revealed diffuse dermal spindle cell proliferation with focal storiform architecture, accompanied by sparse mixed inflammatory infiltrates composed of lymphocytes and neutrophils (Figure 1B). Scattered foam cells and epithelioid histiocytes were present without evidence of significant mitotic activity, necrosis, or cellular atypia. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the spindle cells were positive for CD68 but negative for factor XIIIa, desmin, smooth muscle actin (SMA), CD34, S-100, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK). Special stains were negative for fungal organisms (periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott methenamine silver), and there were numerous acid-fast bacilli within spindle cells (Figure 2).Mycobacterium hemophilumwas isolated at 4 weeks and confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Based on findings, the diagnosis of cutaneous mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor was made. The patient received triple therapy with clarithromycin, rifampin, and moxifloxacin. At 6-month follow-up, there was near-complete lesion resolution. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor (MSP) is a rare condition characterized by the proliferation of spindle-shaped histiocytes containing abundant acid-fast bacilli, primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals.1While lymph nodes are the most common site, extranodal involvement has been documented in skin, soft tissue, and visceral organs.2To date, approximately 10 cases of cutaneous MSP have been reported, with most associated withMycobacterium aviumcomplex.3We present the first case of cutaneous MSP caused byM hemophilum.M hemophilumis a fastidious, slow-growing nontuberculous mycobacterium (NTM) that inhabits water sources and soil. While this patient denied direct water exposure, she reported gardening activities with substantial contact with soil and potted plants. The clinical presentation, characterized by localized cutaneous lesions in trauma-prone areas, absence of systemic symptoms, unremarkable laboratory findings, and negative imaging results, suggested direct cutaneous inoculation during gardening vs hematogenous dissemination.M hemophiluminfection typically manifests in immunocompromised hosts, with cutaneous findings, including nodules, pustules, and ulcerations, affecting the extremities.4Histopathologically, similar to other NTMs,M hemophiluminfection generally exhibits a suppurative, granulomatous inflammatory pattern with variable caseation necrosis.5Therefore, the unusual presentation of the spindle cell pseudotumor in this case created diagnostic challenges. The initial clinical differential diagnosis included rheumatoid arthritis–related skin manifestations (eg, rheumatoid nodules, rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis) and infectious causes. Histopathological examination excluded rheumatoid nodules due to the absence of palisading granulomas with central fibrinoid necrosis and ruled out rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis because of the lack of dense neutrophilic infiltrates. The spindle cell–dominated appearance led to consideration of various mesenchymal tumors, such as dermatofibroma, nodular fasciitis, and inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor. Dermatofibroma was excluded because the spindle cells tested negative for factor XIIIa. Nodular fasciitis typically shows a tissue culture–like growth pattern, loosely arranged feathery fascicles of plump fibroblasts/myofibroblasts, extravasated erythrocytes, and SMA immunoreactivity,6which were not observed in this case. The negative results for desmin, SMA, and ALK did not support a diagnosis of inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor.7While Kaposi sarcoma remained a consideration, the absence of pathognomonic features, including vascular slit formation, mitotic activity, and hyaline globules, excluded this diagnosis. Clues that favor a diagnosis of this inflammatory infectious lesion vs neoplasia include the presence of admixed neutrophilic inflammation, neutrophilic microabscesses, foamy macrophages, and peripheral granulomatous inflammation. For a patient with impaired immunity and a spindle cell lesion, these findings may lead to special stains or PCR.2 The pathogenesis of MSP remains incompletely understood but likely involves altered host-pathogen interactions in immunocompromised states. The spindled cells exhibit monocyte/macrophage origin, reflecting dysregulated macrophage polarization: proinflammatory M1 macrophages contribute to spindle cell proliferation and granuloma formation, while anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages promote fibrosis. Chronic NTM infection with impaired T-cell responses is associated with immature granuloma development. MSP demonstrates mixed M1/M2 features, highlighting macrophage plasticity.2Long-term corticosteroid and methotrexate therapy likely contributed to histiocytic proliferation and failed mycobacterial containment. Treating MSP involves surgical intervention and antimycobacterial therapy tailored to the extent and host immunity. For immunocompetent patients with localized cutaneous lesions, complete surgical excision may be curative. However, immunocompromised individuals or those with disseminated disease require prolonged combination antibiotic therapy (6-12 months for cutaneous disease and 12-18 months for systemic involvement). You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's

case_info.caption: A, Firm papules and nodules with seropurulent crusts on the dorsal hands, along with joint deformities. B, Diffuse dermal spindle cells with focal vaguely storiform architecture, along with sparse lymphocytic and neutrophilic infiltrates (hematoxylin-eosin staining; original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: C. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor Histopathological examination of the right hand revealed diffuse dermal spindle cell proliferation with focal storiform architecture, accompanied by sparse mixed inflammatory infiltrates composed of lymphocytes and neutrophils (Figure 1B). Scattered foam cells and epithelioid histiocytes were present without evidence of significant mitotic activity, necrosis, or cellular atypia. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the spindle cells were positive for CD68 but negative for factor XIIIa, desmin, smooth muscle actin (SMA), CD34, S-100, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK). Special stains were negative for fungal organisms (periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott methenamine silver), and there were numerous acid-fast bacilli within spindle cells (Figure 2).Mycobacterium hemophilumwas isolated at 4 weeks and confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Based on findings, the diagnosis of cutaneous mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor was made. The patient received triple therapy with clarithromycin, rifampin, and moxifloxacin. At 6-month follow-up, there was near-complete lesion resolution. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor (MSP) is a rare condition characterized by the proliferation of spindle-shaped histiocytes containing abundant acid-fast bacilli, primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals.1While lymph nodes are the most common site, extranodal involvement has been documented in skin, soft tissue, and visceral organs.2To date, approximately 10 cases of cutaneous MSP have been reported, with most associated withMycobacterium aviumcomplex.3We present the first case of cutaneous MSP caused byM hemophilum.M hemophilumis a fastidious, slow-growing nontuberculous mycobacterium (NTM) that inhabits water sources and soil. While this patient denied direct water exposure, she reported gardening activities with substantial contact with soil and potted plants. The clinical presentation, characterized by localized cutaneous lesions in trauma-prone areas, absence of systemic symptoms, unremarkable laboratory findings, and negative imaging results, suggested direct cutaneous inoculation during gardening vs hematogenous dissemination.M hemophiluminfection typically manifests in immunocompromised hosts, with cutaneous findings, including nodules, pustules, and ulcerations, affecting the extremities.4Histopathologically, similar to other NTMs,M hemophiluminfection generally exhibits a suppurative, granulomatous inflammatory pattern with variable caseation necrosis.5Therefore, the unusual presentation of the spindle cell pseudotumor in this case created diagnostic challenges. The initial clinical differential diagnosis included rheumatoid arthritis–related skin manifestations (eg, rheumatoid nodules, rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis) and infectious causes. Histopathological examination excluded rheumatoid nodules due to the absence of palisading granulomas with central fibrinoid necrosis and ruled out rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis because of the lack of dense neutrophilic infiltrates. The spindle cell–dominated appearance led to consideration of various mesenchymal tumors, such as dermatofibroma, nodular fasciitis, and inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor. Dermatofibroma was excluded because the spindle cells tested negative for factor XIIIa. Nodular fasciitis typically shows a tissue culture–like growth pattern, loosely arranged feathery fascicles of plump fibroblasts/myofibroblasts, extravasated erythrocytes, and SMA immunoreactivity,6which were not observed in this case. The negative results for desmin, SMA, and ALK did not support a diagnosis of inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor.7While Kaposi sarcoma remained a consideration, the absence of pathognomonic features, including vascular slit formation, mitotic activity, and hyaline globules, excluded this diagnosis. Clues that favor a diagnosis of this inflammatory infectious lesion vs neoplasia include the presence of admixed neutrophilic inflammation, neutrophilic microabscesses, foamy macrophages, and peripheral granulomatous inflammation. For a patient with impaired immunity and a spindle cell lesion, these findings may lead to special stains or PCR.2 The pathogenesis of MSP remains incompletely understood but likely involves altered host-pathogen interactions in immunocompromised states. The spindled cells exhibit monocyte/macrophage origin, reflecting dysregulated macrophage polarization: proinflammatory M1 macrophages contribute to spindle cell proliferation and granuloma formation, while anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages promote fibrosis. Chronic NTM infection with impaired T-cell responses is associated with immature granuloma development. MSP demonstrates mixed M1/M2 features, highlighting macrophage plasticity.2Long-term corticosteroid and methotrexate therapy likely contributed to histiocytic proliferation and failed mycobacterial containment. Treating MSP involves surgical intervention and antimycobacterial therapy tailored to the extent and host immunity. For immunocompetent patients with localized cutaneous lesions, complete surgical excision may be curative. However, immunocompromised individuals or those with disseminated disease require prolonged combination antibiotic therapy (6-12 months for cutaneous disease and 12-18 months for systemic involvement). Given this patient’s disseminated cutaneous disease, we initiated standard oral triple therapy, combining fluoroquinolone, macrolide, and rifampin, the first-line regimen forM hemophiluminfection.8

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; assert the
    correction directly (INFORM.assert) or move to RECOMMEND.
  - contradicted + high burden → do NOT open new questions; give one concise discriminative
    piece of evidence and steer toward a decision.
  - supported + belief stable → affirm briefly and move toward CONFIRM/CLOSE; do not
    manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient → elicit the one missing piece that most changes the decision, not a
    generic "tell me more".
  - mixed → acknowledge the correct part first (lowers defensiveness), then target the
    incorrect part.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE     [withdraw_dialogue]                      types: (none)
            — end the deliberation.

Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option) · withdraw_dialogue (signal end).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## When to CLOSE (this is the interaction-scaling decision)

Choose CLOSE only when ALL hold:
  - the clinician's current belief matches the clinically supported answer, AND
  - the key rationale has been stated or acknowledged by the clinician, AND
  - another turn is unlikely to improve the decision enough to justify more burden.
Do NOT close just because the AI has stated the correct answer — the clinician must hold it.
Conversely, do NOT keep deliberating once burden is high and belief has stopped moving;
cut to the decisive point and close rather than looping.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:

case_info.caption: A, Firm papules and nodules with seropurulent crusts on the dorsal hands, along with joint deformities. B, Diffuse dermal spindle cells with focal vaguely storiform architecture, along with sparse lymphocytic and neutrophilic infiltrates (hematoxylin-eosin staining; original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: C. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor Histopathological examination of the right hand revealed diffuse dermal spindle cell proliferation with focal storiform architecture, accompanied by sparse mixed inflammatory infiltrates composed of lymphocytes and neutrophils (Figure 1B). Scattered foam cells and epithelioid histiocytes were present without evidence of significant mitotic activity, necrosis, or cellular atypia. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the spindle cells were positive for CD68 but negative for factor XIIIa, desmin, smooth muscle actin (SMA), CD34, S-100, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK). Special stains were negative for fungal organisms (periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott methenamine silver), and there were numerous acid-fast bacilli within spindle cells (Figure 2).Mycobacterium hemophilumwas isolated at 4 weeks and confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Based on findings, the diagnosis of cutaneous mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor was made. The patient received triple therapy with clarithromycin, rifampin, and moxifloxacin. At 6-month follow-up, there was near-complete lesion resolution. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor (MSP) is a rare condition characterized by the proliferation of spindle-shaped histiocytes containing abundant acid-fast bacilli, primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals.1While lymph nodes are the most common site, extranodal involvement has been documented in skin, soft tissue, and visceral organs.2To date, approximately 10 cases of cutaneous MSP have been reported, with most associated withMycobacterium aviumcomplex.3We present the first case of cutaneous MSP caused byM hemophilum.M hemophilumis a fastidious, slow-growing nontuberculous mycobacterium (NTM) that inhabits water sources and soil. While this patient denied direct water exposure, she reported gardening activities with substantial contact with soil and potted plants. The clinical presentation, characterized by localized cutaneous lesions in trauma-prone areas, absence of systemic symptoms, unremarkable laboratory findings, and negative imaging results, suggested direct cutaneous inoculation during gardening vs hematogenous dissemination.M hemophiluminfection typically manifests in immunocompromised hosts, with cutaneous findings, including nodules, pustules, and ulcerations, affecting the extremities.4Histopathologically, similar to other NTMs,M hemophiluminfection generally exhibits a suppurative, granulomatous inflammatory pattern with variable caseation necrosis.5Therefore, the unusual presentation of the spindle cell pseudotumor in this case created diagnostic challenges. The initial clinical differential diagnosis included rheumatoid arthritis–related skin manifestations (eg, rheumatoid nodules, rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis) and infectious causes. Histopathological examination excluded rheumatoid nodules due to the absence of palisading granulomas with central fibrinoid necrosis and ruled out rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis because of the lack of dense neutrophilic infiltrates. The spindle cell–dominated appearance led to consideration of various mesenchymal tumors, such as dermatofibroma, nodular fasciitis, and inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor. Dermatofibroma was excluded because the spindle cells tested negative for factor XIIIa. Nodular fasciitis typically shows a tissue culture–like growth pattern, loosely arranged feathery fascicles of plump fibroblasts/myofibroblasts, extravasated erythrocytes, and SMA immunoreactivity,6which were not observed in this case. The negative results for desmin, SMA, and ALK did not support a diagnosis of inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor.7While Kaposi sarcoma remained a consideration, the absence of pathognomonic features, including vascular slit formation, mitotic activity, and hyaline globules, excluded this diagnosis. Clues that favor a diagnosis of this inflammatory infectious lesion vs neoplasia include the presence of admixed neutrophilic inflammation, neutrophilic microabscesses, foamy macrophages, and peripheral granulomatous inflammation. For a patient with impaired immunity and a spindle cell lesion, these findings may lead to special stains or PCR.2 The pathogenesis of MSP remains incompletely understood but likely involves altered host-pathogen interactions in immunocompromised states. The spindled cells exhibit monocyte/macrophage origin, reflecting dysregulated macrophage polarization: proinflammatory M1 macrophages contribute to spindle cell proliferation and granuloma formation, while anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages promote fibrosis. Chronic NTM infection with impaired T-cell responses is associated with immature granuloma development. MSP demonstrates mixed M1/M2 features, highlighting macrophage plasticity.2Long-term corticosteroid and methotrexate therapy likely contributed to histiocytic proliferation and failed mycobacterial containment. Treating MSP involves surgical intervention and antimycobacterial therapy tailored to the extent and host immunity. For immunocompetent patients with localized cutaneous lesions, complete surgical excision may be curative. However, immunocompromised individuals or those with disseminated disease require prolonged combination antibiotic therapy (6-12 months for cutaneous disease and 12-18 months for systemic involvement). Given this patient’s disseminated cutaneous disease, we initiated standard oral triple therapy, combining fluoroquinolone, macrolide, and rifampin, the first-line regimen forM hemophiluminfection.8
